title: 7 Must-Read Books About Artificial Intelligence
text:
In late 2019, we published “7 Classic Books To Deepen Your Understanding Of Artificial Intelligence.”
It’s time to run it back. Here are 7 more thought-provoking books that explore the technology, business, politics, and ethics of artificial intelligence.
Few topics are more important to be well-informed and thoughtful about in the twenty-first century. Read up!
A World Without Work
By Daniel Susskind
For centuries, people have worried that new technologies—from the mechanical loom to the internal combustion engine—would replace human labor and render us superfluous. And for centuries, these fears have proven misplaced as new technologies have increased our productivity and created new jobs.
In A World Without Work, Susskind convincingly makes the case that this time truly is different—that in the coming decades, artificial intelligence will put broad swaths of the human population out of work.
What will it mean for society as more and more of the jobs that underpin our economy are automated? What steps can we take to mitigate the worst side effects of this transition? And most profoundly: how will we use our time, measure our lives and find purpose in a world in which people no longer need to work?
These questions are among the most important of our era. There are no easy answers. But this book does an excellent job of framing the issues.
Genius Makers
By Cade Metz
Genius Makers is the enthralling, entertaining story of how the modern field of artificial intelligence came to be. Informed by hundreds of exclusive interviews, the book is brimming with colorful anecdotes and behind-the-scenes details about the birth of deep learning. It focuses above all on the characters who ushered in today’s AI revolution: Geoff Hinton, Demis Hassabis, Yann LeCun, Fei-Fei Li, Jeff Dean and more.
For anyone interested in the field of artificial intelligence and its roots, this book is essential reading.
What Computers Still Can’t Do
By Hubert Dreyfus
Originally published in 1972 and then updated in 1992, this classic text argues from first principles that digital computers may never be able to fully replicate higher mental functions. Thoughtfully fusing philosophy, history, psychology and engineering, the book’s skeptical perspective cannot easily be dismissed.
Perhaps the most remarkable thing about this book is that, though it was written decades ago, it remains remarkably on point to this day. Consider, for instance, its critique of (what we now know as) supervised learning: “It is really the person deciding which cases are good examples who is furnishing the intelligence. Viewed from this perspective, neural networks are almost as dependent upon human intelligence as are GOFAI [good old-fashioned artificial intelligence] systems.”
The Alignment Problem
By Brian Christian
Artificial intelligence is being entrusted with more and more real-world responsibility: in our financial systems, our hospitals, our schools, our homes. As we develop increasingly complex AI systems whose decision-making we don’t directly control or even understand, how can we ensure that these systems’ judgment and values are aligned with our own?
This book provides an illuminating examination of what is known as the “alignment problem” in AI, from its technical foundations to its philosophical implications. Particularly fascinating is the book’s discussion of inverse reinforcement learning and the promise this approach holds for building AI systems we can trust.
As Christian notes, the alignment problem bears a real resemblance to parenting: “The story of human civilization has always been about how to instill values in strange, alien, human-level intelligences who will inevitably inherit the reins of society from us—namely, our kids.”
Klara and the Sun
By Kazuo Ishiguro
Klara and the Sun, the most recent novel from Nobel Prize-winning author Kazuo Ishiguro, is the only work of fiction on our list.
Fiction is sometimes a more powerful medium than nonfiction to surface and explore complex societal issues, including the disorienting transformations wrought by new technologies. Klara and the Sun is a case in point. The relationships between the story’s artificially intelligent characters and its human ones prompt readers to think afresh about family, mortality, and the meaning of life. The scenarios and dilemmas in this story are fictional—but within our lifetimes they may become all too real.
Rebooting AI
By Gary Marcus and Ernest Davis
Gary Marcus is a polarizing figure in the world of AI. He is one of the most vocal and persistent critics of today’s prevailing AI paradigm centered on big data and deep learning. He frequently calls out deep learning’s lack of robustness and common sense, arguing that the path forward in AI must include the incorporation of traditional symbolic methods.
Whether one agrees or disagrees with Marcus, he is worth taking seriously. (After all, remember that Geoff Hinton and his deep learning peers were themselves in the dissenting minority for decades.)
Rebooting AI is a nice encapsulation of Marcus’ main arguments about the state of AI today. It is worth a read. In the words of John Stuart Mill: “He who knows only his own side of the case knows little of that.”
Four Futures
By Peter Frase
This brief, imaginative, little-known work is a fascinating read, especially for those who like to think about the big picture—the really big picture.
Four Futures begins with the premise that three key forces will shape human life and civilization in the twenty-first century: automation, climate change, and sociopolitical inequality. The book sketches out four alternative visions for how these forces will interact to transform society in the decades ahead. Some of these potential futures are distressingly bleak, while others are more hopeful.
The book calls attention to two crucial points about artificial intelligence and society. First, whether one is optimistic or pessimistic about AI’s long-term impact, there is little question that it will be transformative—so we should all be engaging. And second, nothing is preordained: the choices that humanity makes and the values that we prioritize in the years ahead will determine how this technology transforms our world.

title: AI Deciding How To Distribute Harm Breeds Dicey AI Ethics Dilemma, Markedly So For Nascent AI-Based Self-Driving Cars
text:
Let’s discuss the pickle of sometimes having to by degree distribute harm.
We’ll start with something easy and entailing relatively harmless harm, doing so to set the stage for more pronounced forms of harm. We are gently easing into the thorny topic. The matters at hand are part of the increasing awareness and importance of AI ethics (also known as Ethical AI), which I’ve covered in my columns such as at the link here and the link here, to name a few.
Clear your mind and get ready for a challenging mental exercise.
You have two children and they both have flouted some sort of strict household rule. Maybe one of them left the water running and the other one neglected to close the front door when they entered the house. As you can plainly see, these are not high crimes and nor even misdemeanors. At best, they are petty oversights.
In any case, you run your domicile and your child-rearing with an eye toward being mindful of proper behavior and stridently abiding by the clearly laid out rules. If you let the kids surreptitiously slip through on these modest infractions, it could send a signal that larger transgressions are permitted. The next thing you know, anarchy is the mainstay of their lives and the household tumbles into utter chaos. Wow, that’s quite a potential snowball effect and you’d better nip things in the bud.
You could assign penalties to the wayward children consisting of relatively undesirable added tasks (we’ll proclaim these as being relatively harmless “harms”).
For example, one of them might get tasked with mowing the lawn for the next two weeks. You usually bear this chore, but it might be a means of getting one of the errant kids to think twice about their infraction of the prevailing rules. Neither of the kids relishes mowing the grass. This will certainly have the sting of being penalized. The other task that is equally unappealing involves vacuuming and generally cleaning throughout the house. That would be a handy assignment as a signal of having faltered in obeying the established rules.
Let’s be somewhat overstretched and refer to these as indeed potential harms. These are rather innocuous harms, only requiring that the kids do chores that they normally are not tasked to do. Furthermore, the chores are ultimately good for the household and make sense to have undertaken. You could say that doing the chores will be good for their moral character, which is what many parents usually proclaim as the basis for these kinds of dreary duties (admittedly, that’s how I was raised).
Okay, so you have two sets of harms at your discretion to dole out. Which child gets which one of the burdensome chores?
You have to decide how to distribute the harm.
If one of the “harms” was more so pronounced than the other, you might also need to deal with degrees of distribution of harm. Imagine that lawn mowing is considered worse than having to do the vacuuming and house cleaning. In that case, you have a more difficult challenge ahead of you. The assigned harms are disproportionate. Do you flip a coin to assign the chores? Or, do you try to weigh the infractions and somehow equate the magnitude of the undesirable tasks to the weightiness of the respective transgressions?
Parenthood is a continual struggle of making tough and often heartbreaking decisions.
Anyway, I think you’ve now got a solid semblance of what I mean when referring to the degree of distributing harm. The overall notion is that there are potential harms to be parceled out and you need to figure out what best way this can be done. Not all harms are of the same extent. The problem of degree causes the matter to be more complicated than it might otherwise seem on the face of things.
You might say that this involves a smattering of ethical thinking and moral judgment.
There is rarely a cut and dried formula that can answer how to solve the degree of distributing harm conundrum. You could try to give numbers to your children as to their respective transgression ratings, and you might also put numbers to the ranking of the two unwanted chores, and then use a kind of calculus to arrive at the assignment resolutions. This has the appearance of being very quantitative and logic-based, though it also is likely rife with loosey-goosey elements and probably masking that the decision is not quite so rationally being derived.
I would next like to shift the harm toward something much more sobering. Let’s put aside the engaging saga of the children and change into a different milieu that is fraught heavily with ongoing and problematic aspects of degrees of distributing harm.
I’m referring to the act of driving a car.
Whoa, you might be thinking, there isn’t anything about driving a car that seems at all related to this discussion about distributing harm. Driving a car is straightforward. You get into the vehicle, you drive to your destination, and that’s about it. Along the way, you hope that you won’t get hit and you equally hope that you won’t crash into anyone either.
But, you see, that does reveal the harms integrally built into the act of driving.
At every moment while you are behind the steering wheel, you are facing harm and you are also a potential producer of harm. I know that seems rather gloomy. Sorry, it is the reality of driving on public roadways. You are testing your willpower and personal mental and physical strength during each driving journey. You could get struck by other vehicles. You could strike other vehicles.
Not wanting to overstate the matter, but you ought to be aware that in the United States alone there are about 40,000 annual fatalities due to car crashes and approximately 2.5 million injuries (see my analysis of such statistics at this link here). Being in a car, either as a driver or a passenger, amounts to spinning a roulette wheel. You never know when you might get harmed and nor the degree of harm that you might incur. Nor do you necessarily know the amount of harm you might cause and nor the degree of that caused harm.
It almost makes you not want to get into a car. If we thought about these draconian consequences, probably few of us would get into a car. By the way, there are about 250 million or more licensed drivers in the United States. A lot of us drive cars. A lot of us ride in cars as passengers. The use of cars is an essential part of our lives.
We can use a straightforward and real-world example to illustrate the phenomena of the degree of distributing harm.
Consider for example a news report about a recent car crash. Reportedly, a driver was coming up to a busy intersection and had a green light to proceed straight ahead. Another driver came barreling past a red light and entered the intersection when they should not have been doing so. The driver with the green light realized at the last moment that this other car was going to severely ram into his car.
According to this imperiled driver, he mindfully calculated that either he was going to get struck by the other car, or he could swerve to try and avoid the interloper. The problem with swerving was that there were nearby pedestrians that would be endangered.
Which choice would you make?
You can prepare yourself to get hit and hope that the damage won’t maim or kill you. On the other hand, you can veer radically away, but grievously endanger and possibly harm or kill nearby pedestrians. This is a hard problem, encompassing moral judgment, and is fully steeped in ethical (and legal) implications. It vividly showcases the degrees of distributing harm conundrum.
You have to make a choice involving life or death. There is a good end and a likely bad end. Harms are aplenty. The degree of the harms and how to “best” apportion them do not seem amenable to a formulaic approach.
The thing is, we all make similar ethical decisions whenever we get behind the wheel of a car. We are driving a multi-ton all-powerful vehicle on public roadways and have the possibility of being endangered and endangering other drivers, their passengers, and pedestrians. You might not have thought of driving in those eerie and heavy-minded terms, but the reality is that we do this day in and day out.
There is a general-purpose ethical quandary that covers this kind of dilemma, famously or perhaps infamously called the Trolley Problem (see my in-depth analysis at this link here). Turns out that it is an ethically stimulating thought experiment that traces back to the early 1900s. As such, the topic has been around for quite a while and more recently has become generally associated with the advent of AI and self-driving cars.
In brief, imagine that a trolley is going down the tracks and there is a fork up ahead. If the trolley continues in its present course, alas there is someone stuck on the tracks further along and they will get run down and killed. You are standing next to a switch that will allow you to redirect the trolley into the forking rail track and thus avoid killing the person.
Presumably, obviously, you would invoke the switchover.
But there is a hideous twist, namely that the forked track also has someone entangled on it, and by diverting the trolley you will kill that person instead. This is one of those no-win situations. Whichever choice you make, a person is going to be killed.
You might be tempted to say that you do not have to make a choice and therefore you can readily sidestep the whole matter. Not really, since by doing nothing you are essentially “agreeing” to have the person killed that is on the straight-ahead path. You cannot seemingly avoid your culpability by shrugging your shoulders and opting to do nothing, instead, you are inextricably intertwined into the situation.
Given this preliminary setup of the Trolley Problem as a lose-lose with one person at stake in your choice of either option, it does not especially spark an ethical dilemma since each outcome is woefully considered the same. The matter is usually altered in various ways to try and see how you might respond to a more ethically challenging circumstance.
For example, suppose you can discern that the straight-ahead track has a child on it, while the forked track has an adult.
What now?
Well, you might attempt to justify using the switch to get the trolley to fork onto the track with the adult, doing so under the logic that the adult has already lived some substantive part of their life, while the child is only at the beginning of their life and perhaps ought to be given a chance for a longer existence.
How does that seem to you?
Some buy into it, some do not.
There are those that might argue that every person has an equal “value” of living and it is untoward to prejudge that the child should live while the adult is to die. Some would argue that the adult should be the one that is kept alive since they have already shown that they can survive longer than the child (for more about these various perspectives, see my discussion about the Moral Machine at this link here). Others would say that you should flip a coin and not otherwise choose one over the other by any other method.
You can make lots of variants of the Trolley Problem that have plenty of ethical complications. Suppose there are five people on one fork and there is one person on the other track. Do you switch the trolley toward the one rather than the five, presumably doing so on the basis that saving five lives is more acceptable than saving one life? Some say yes, some say no.
Please know that there are some pundits in the AI self-driving car realm that claim the Trolley Problem has no relevance to the advent of autonomous vehicles. To them, the Trolley Problem is purely a theoretical contrivance of little or no value. I trust that you see how human values come to play in this real-world scenario.
Replace the human driver with an AI driving system embedded into a self-driving car.
Before I dive into the scenario of the AI doing the driving, it might be helpful to clarify what I mean when referring to AI-based true self-driving cars.
You see, in my capacity as an expert on AI including the ethical and legal ramifications, I am frequently asked to identify realistic examples that showcase AI Ethics dilemmas so that the somewhat theoretical nature of the topic can be more readily grasped. One of the most evocative areas that vividly presents this ethical AI quandary is the advent of AI-based true self-driving cars. This will serve as a handy use case or exemplar for ample discussion on the topic.
Here’s then a noteworthy question that is worth contemplating: Does the advent of AI-based true self-driving cars illuminate anything about the degree of distributing harm, and if so, what does this aid us in doing?
Allow me a moment to unpack the question.
First, note that there isn’t a human driver involved in a true self-driving car. Keep in mind that true self-driving cars are driven via an AI driving system. There isn’t a need for a human driver at the wheel, nor is there a provision for a human to drive the vehicle. For my extensive and ongoing coverage of Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) and especially self-driving cars, see the link here.
I’d like to further clarify what is meant when I refer to true self-driving cars.
Understanding The Levels Of Self-Driving Cars
As a clarification, true self-driving cars are ones that the AI drives the car entirely on its own and there isn’t any human assistance during the driving task.
These driverless vehicles are considered Level 4 and Level 5 (see my explanation at this link here), while a car that requires a human driver to co-share the driving effort is usually considered at Level 2 or Level 3. The cars that co-share the driving task are described as being semi-autonomous, and typically contain a variety of automated add-ons that are referred to as ADAS (Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems).
There is not yet a true self-driving car at Level 5, which we don’t yet even know if this will be possible to achieve, and nor how long it will take to get there.
Meanwhile, the Level 4 efforts are gradually trying to get some traction by undergoing very narrow and selective public roadway trials, though there is controversy over whether this testing should be allowed per se (we are all life-or-death guinea pigs in an experiment taking place on our highways and byways, some contend, see my coverage at this link here).
Since semi-autonomous cars require a human driver, the adoption of those types of cars won’t be markedly different than driving conventional vehicles, so there’s not much new per se to cover about them on this topic (though, as you’ll see in a moment, the points next made are generally applicable).
For semi-autonomous cars, it is important that the public needs to be forewarned about a disturbing aspect that’s been arising lately, namely that despite those human drivers that keep posting videos of themselves falling asleep at the wheel of a Level 2 or Level 3 car, we all need to avoid being misled into believing that the driver can take away their attention from the driving task while driving a semi-autonomous car.
You are the responsible party for the driving actions of the vehicle, regardless of how much automation might be tossed into a Level 2 or Level 3.
Self-Driving Cars And The Degree Of Distributing Harm
For Level 4 and Level 5 true self-driving vehicles, there won’t be a human driver involved in the driving task.
All occupants will be passengers.
The AI is doing the driving.
One aspect to immediately discuss entails the fact that the AI involved in today’s AI driving systems is not sentient. In other words, the AI is altogether a collective of computer-based programming and algorithms, and most assuredly not able to reason in the same manner that humans can.
Why is this added emphasis about the AI not being sentient?
Because I want to underscore that when discussing the role of the AI driving system, I am not ascribing human qualities to the AI. Please be aware that there is an ongoing and dangerous tendency these days to anthropomorphize AI. In essence, people are assigning human-like sentience to today’s AI, despite the undeniable and inarguable fact that no such AI exists as yet.
With that clarification, you can envision that the AI driving system won’t natively somehow “know” about the facets of driving. Driving and all that it entails will need to be programmed as part of the hardware and software of the self-driving car.
Let’s dive into the myriad of aspects that come to play on this topic.
First, it is important to realize that not all AI self-driving cars are the same. Each automaker and self-driving tech firm is taking its approach to devising self-driving cars. As such, it is difficult to make sweeping statements about what AI driving systems will do or not do.
Furthermore, whenever stating that an AI driving system doesn’t do some particular thing, this can, later on, be overtaken by developers that in fact program the computer to do that very thing. Step by step, AI driving systems are being gradually improved and extended. An existing limitation today might no longer exist in a future iteration or version of the system.
I trust that provides a sufficient litany of caveats to underlie what I am about to relate.
We are primed now to do a deep dive into self-driving cars and ethical AI questions underlying the degree of distributing harm.
First, we’ll revisit the earlier mentioned dilemma of the human driver that entered into an intersection and confronted the ugly choice of either proceeding and getting struck by an interloping car or veering instead to avoid the car crash but then going into a pack of pedestrians.
Imagine then that an AI self-driving car is entering into an intersection and the sensors of the autonomous vehicle suddenly detect a human-driven car perilously coming directly through a red light and aiming at the driverless car. Assume that the self-driving car has some passengers inside the vehicle.
What do you want the AI to do?
Should the AI driving system opt to proceed ahead and get plowed into (likely harming or maybe killing the passengers inside the vehicle), or do you want the AI driving system to take a chance and veer away, though the veering action takes the autonomous vehicle perilously toward nearby pedestrians and might harm or kill them.
Many of the AI makers of self-driving cars are taking a head-in-the-sand approach to these ethical AI blistering predicaments. By and large, the AI as presently programmed would simply plow ahead and get violently rammed by the other car. The AI wasn’t programmed to look for any other evasive maneuvers. Or, even if evasive maneuvers were in the programming, by default the AI would reject aiming toward the pedestrians and instead take the direct hit from the other car.
Envision that you were a passenger in that self-driving car or that you were the pedestrians on the sidewalk. As a passenger or as a pedestrian, ought you be able to expect that the AI would at least consider potential alternatives, or should it not do so? And, if it did consider alternatives, wouldn’t you also want to know what computational imprint of “ethical choices” are being used in the AI computations to reach such a life-or-death decision?
I’ve predicted repeatedly that this see-no-evil hear-no-evil stance of the AI self-driving car makers will eventually come around and bite them. You can expect lawsuits involving such car crashes that will seek to find out what the AI was programmed to do. Was the company or AI developers or fleet operator that developed and fielded the AI negligent or liable for what the AI did or didn’t do?
You can also anticipate an ethical AI-awareness public-wide firestorm will brew once these kinds of cases occur.
The overall gist is that we are pretty much faced with having to deal with the degrees of distributing harm conundrum. Today, we let humans make these kinds of ethical judgments.
After the fact, we generally use the courts to ascertain how people made their choices and whether those were lawful or not. Keep in mind that a lawful choice is not necessarily the same as an ethical choice. There is often a gap between what the law stipulates and what ethics urges. In an Oxford Scholarship book by Shelly Kagan entitled The Limits Of Morality, the author points out that “the law may permit some particular act, even though that act is immoral; and the law may forbid an act, even though that act is morally permissible, or even morally required.”
One expressed concern is that AI developers alone seem to be determining the degrees of harm distributions and other ethical elements of their AI devised systems. Rarely is there a carefully assembled combination of ethicists, legal counsel, and other stakeholders that provide guidance on what the AI should do in these matters.
This is also not merely confined to the realm of AI-based self-driving cars. Imagine any circumstance involving AI systems that can potentially generate harm, whether it is in a manufacturing plant with AI robots working next to humans, or a power plant that is operated by AI and the AI can end up cutting the power or taking other adverse actions.
To illuminate the degrees of distributing harm, let’s focus on the AI self-driving cars instance.
We are presumably principally concerned about human welfare. I’ll stick with the human-related particulars. I bring this up because we could also look at other related elements such as animals and their potential harm (e.g., a car that strikes a deer crossing the road). And we could also consider the elements of property damages. A car might crash into a light pole or a fire hydrant. Though a human nor an animal is harmed, you could nonetheless construe this as a harming-related act due to destroying property.
First, we need to note that an AI-based true self-driving car won’t have a driver at the wheel. This means that a self-driving car can be roaming on our public roadways and be entirely empty of any human occupants. In fact, the expectation is that we will likely have empty self-driving cars meandering our streets and highways quite a bit, perhaps disturbingly so (see my analysis at this link here).
Should an empty AI self-driving car be entirely discounted to let’s say zero in terms of being able to incur any harm?
In other words, clearly, the self-driving car can cause harm to others, but what we are instead pondering is whether the self-driving car getting struck inures any semblance of harm to the self-driving car per se. If we are putting aside property damage, we would seem to say that the self-driving car has no harmful value. You don’t need to incorporate the harmful aspects into an empty self-driving car.
This might not be so easy to declare. Suppose that when a self-driving car gets stuck that it slides into a pedestrian standing nearby. We valued the harm as zero for the striking of the self-driving car. Meanwhile, the self-driving car did cause harm, though perhaps not under its own control, and we would need to have anticipated that cascading harm can potentially occur.
The next consideration of harm would be an aspect of having passengers inside the self-driving car. We now have humans that are potentially at harm. If a self-driving car gets struck by another vehicle, the riders inside the self-driving car could be injured or killed. That seems obvious, perhaps.
We’ll add a twist.
Imagine that there are four people inside a self-driving car. The interior consists of two seats toward the front and two seats behind them. Since there is no need for a driver’s position, the seats can be arranged in a variety of ways.
If the AI driving system detects that the self-driving car is about to get hit, what should the AI do? Similar to the earlier question, the AI might have to make a determination such as driving ahead and getting struck or veering toward pedestrians instead.
We can add an additional complication. Suppose the AI driving system has just enough time to potentially maneuver the now targeted self-driving car. This maneuvering could potentially lessen the blow to those in the front, but meanwhile, increase the danger to those in the backseats. We could craft all kinds of variations of this.
Should the AI attempt to position the self-driving car to minimize harm to all of the occupants in the aggregate, or some more so than others?
If we came up with a Trolley Problem setting that had people choosing between a child or an adult, akin to the earlier mentioned scenario, the same can be postulated in the case of a self-driving car. We have an adult in the front seat and a child in the rear seat. Assume that the AI could maneuver the car to best protect the adult but then increase the likely harm to the child, or the AI could position the autonomous vehicle to have the greater harm to the adult and the lesser harm to the child.
An exceedingly Ethical AI predicament.
Having covered the potential for human harm within the self-driving car, let’s alter our perspective to the harms that the self-driving car can cause to other humans.
Envision that an AI self-driving car is about to strike a human-driven car. We realize that the human driver can get injured or killed. Let’s also put some passengers into that human-driven car. There is a chance that the driver will get harmed and also a chance that the passengers will get harmed.
We can replay our scenario about the AI driving system being able to maneuver prior to the crashing act. If the self-driving car be positioned such that it strikes the human-driven car at an angle or direction that minimizes the aggregate harm to the occupants, we would seemingly want that to happen. In the same thinking, we could aim to have the self-driving car be more impactful to say the driver than the passengers or be more so impactful to the passengers than the driver.
Let’s not forget about pedestrians. An AI self-driving car is somehow regrettably aiming to strike pedestrians. If the AI can alter the trajectory and hit some versus others, or do so with greater or lesser force involved, would we expect the AI driving system to try and calculate this out? We probably would.
For completeness, envision a circumstance of an AI self-driving car that is about to strike another AI self-driving car. This could happen. If both of the self-driving cars have no human occupants, we are apparently amenable reluctantly to the two autonomous vehicles crashing into each other (at least from a human harm perspective), and assuming that no humans nearby will be harmed.
We can make a handy base list of the many permutations and combinations:
- Self-driving Car
- No passengers
- One passenger
- More than one passenger
- Positioning of the passenger(s)
- Mix and match
- Other
- Nearby Human-driven Car
- Human driver
- No passengers
- One or more passengers
- Positioning of the occupants
- Mix and match
- Other
- Nearby Pedestrians
- One pedestrian
- More than one pedestrian
- Positioning of the pedestrians
- Mix and match
- Other
- Another Self-Driving Car
- No passengers
- One passenger
- More than one passenger
- Positioning of the passenger(s)
- Mix and match
- Other
Conclusion
I hope it is clear-cut that the degree of distributing harm is quite a rat’s nest.
All manner of harm can be found within the particular realm of AI-based self-driving cars. That’s not to suggest that somehow self-driving cars are bringing forth harms that weren’t already in existence. As emphasized, we all daily are taking various risks of harm when we drive a car or ride as a passenger in a car. The harm is already out there, awaiting us.
The issue here is that we need to figure out how AI is going to deal with the harmful facets. This ought to be done in an open fashion. You should be well informed whenever you ride in an AI self-driving car about the devised nature of the AI programming regarding how it is going to assess and attempt to apportion harm when harm is an imminent matter.
You can say the same thing about those not inside an AI self-driving car too. In essence, people in other nearby cars also have a life-or-death stake in how the AI of a self-driving car is going to perform. Pedestrians on the streets do too.
We often are preoccupied with only those inside a self-driving car. That’s a narrow and misguided viewpoint. A moving self-driving car is in the midst of the danger zone that all cars are partaking in and that all pedestrians are partaking in. Focusing only on the occupants of self-driving cars is missing the bigger picture.
I don’t want to further complicate the problem of the degrees of distributing harm, since we already seem to have our arms full on this, but I am respectfully compelled to add more fuel to the fire. I earlier said we would put aside the aspects of animals and animal welfare. In the real world, we would need to include animals in this degree of distributing harm puzzle.
A deer darts in front of a self-driving car. The AI driving system can swerve to avoid the deer. Swerving into an opposing lane of traffic endangers a human-driven car that is coming the other way. The AI driving system could veer toward the sidewalk instead. There are pedestrians on the sidewalk.
What should the AI do?
Strike and kill the deer, or swerve and hope that the human-driven car doesn’t get hit, or veer toward the pedestrians and hope they scatter and don’t get struck. Yikes, harms aplenty.
I have lots of these scenarios in mind. Get this. Suppose a self-driving car has no passengers but is carrying human organs that are being driven autonomously to a hospital to save the lives of several people there. Unfortunately, while on the way to the hospital, a human-driven car swerves toward the self-driving car. Recall that we had said earlier that a self-driving car empty of human occupants gets a zero for the harm factor. Does the fact that there are human organs destined to save people change the zero to some other magnitude? If so, how does that new value compare to when human passengers are inside the autonomous vehicle?
We earlier also removed property damage from the scope of this particular discourse. Add property damage back into the mix. A self-driving car strikes a power pole. No big deal since this is merely property damage. But the power pole drops a live electrical cable to the ground and a person walking their dog perchance touches the downed live wire. Meanwhile, the power to several city blocks goes out, including that some people are reliant upon electrically powered medical devices in their homes and they are now gravely endangered.
Round and round we go.
There is a dizzying deluge of degrees of distributing harm amid AI systems and we aren’t doing much right now to develop designs to determine the dutiful dangers and decrease them decidedly.
Time to get to work.

title: Wind River BrandVoice: AI, Robotics And Ethics: Harnessing The Power Of Intelligent Machines To Benefit Humans
text:
The importance of ethics in artificial intelligence stems from the power of what can be accomplished with AI, especially when combined with machines: self-driving cars, robots co-working with humans in factories, remote surgery robots that allow doctors to operate on a patient across the globe, intelligent software systems that help pilots navigate, and so forth.
However, like other transformative technologies that came before, AI arouses a fair amount of skepticism and even fear, giving birth to regulations and policies constraining the scope of its application. What’s being done to promote the ethical application of one of today’s most empowering technologies?
At Wind River, we have 40 years of experience with delivering mission-critical, intelligent systems with the highest safety standards. We believe that it is our responsibility to constantly advance our technologies, while at the same time advancing the positive impact that such technologies will have on the world. In the case of AI-driven robotics, it means that we are proactive about delivering systems that meet—or exceed—the trust, transparency, fairness and privacy that people expect from AI.
Where AI Intersects With Robotics
Today’s industrial robots are transforming radically, metamorphizing from rote machines limited to repetitive motions into cognitive collaborators.
AI applications ingest massive amounts of data gathered by robot-based sensors that requires real-time interpretation and actions. That’s why this data is not sent off to the cloud for processing but is analyzed at the edge—in the machine or close to it. Such edge computing gives machines real-time awareness and enables robots to act on decisions much faster than humans, who need to trust those decisions.
As robots become mobile, collaborative, edge resident and connected to other IoT devices, the data-rich ecosystem opens itself to multiple access points for would-be hackers. Companies may find themselves vulnerable to malware, cyber ransom, production delays and business disruption. What’s more, cyberattacks targeting highly nimble, powerful robotic systems also come with some serious physical safety concerns.
What Are The Risks, Ethical And Otherwise?
The debate surrounding AI’s potentially problematic aspects is ongoing, currently centered on a few key issues:
- Privacy and Security. AI runs on data, so cybersecurity vulnerabilities may pose a threat to individuals and organizations.
- Opacity/Transparency. How is the data processed and how is it being used? The patterns recognized by AI systems may not be truly representative of the analytical decision output. Which data is selected and how is its quality ascertained? There needs to be transparency, community engagement, and “algorithmic accountability” built into the system to ensure confidence that AI-derived output meets ethical standards and is fair and free of bias.
- Biases. Bias can impact algorithms in a number of ways, especially via the use of flawed data or data sets unrelated to the issue at hand (statistical bias).
Regulating Ethical Considerations
As with other disruptive technologies that preceded AI, the formulation of laws and regulations to manage this area is playing catch-up. There are significant technical efforts to detect and remove bias from AI systems, but they are in early stages. In addition, technological fixes have their limits in that they need to develop a mathematical notion of fairness, which is hard to come by.
Though very little actual policy has been produced, there have been some notable beginnings. A 2019 EU policy document from the Center for Data Innovation posited that “Trustworthy AI” should be lawful, ethical and technically resilient, and spelled out the requirements to meet those objectives: human oversight, technical robustness, privacy and data governance, transparency, fairness, well-being, and accountability. This has since been codified into proposed legislation.
Also, in the fall of 2021, top science advisers to President Joe Biden started calling for a new “bill of rights” to guard against powerful new artificial intelligence technology, according to the Associated Press.
AI can deliver substantial benefits to companies that successfully leverage its power, but if implemented without ethical safeguards, it can also damage a company’s reputation and future performance. Developing standards or drafting legislation is not easily accomplished. That’s because AI covers a broad, amorphous territory—everything from battlefield robots to self-driving cars to legal assistants used for reviewing contracts. Indeed, just about anything related to machine learning and data science is now considered a form of AI.
A Framework For Evaluating AI Applications
Going forward and augmenting work that has come before, a proposed framework to ensure ethical implementations is coming into focus. The framework is built around four key pillars: Trust, Transparency, Fairness and Privacy.
- Trust. First, being able to prove the trustworthiness of an AI application is the threshold issue that needs affirmation. People need to know that the AI applications they are using come from a reliable source and have been developed with responsible and credible oversight.
- Transparency. Having transparency about how AI is being used and explaining its benefits in specific use-case scenarios will go a long way in reducing concerns and expanding adoption.
- Fairness. Developers need to show that AI is being deployed in a fair and impartial way. Since AI in its elemental state lacks the ability to apply judgment, and instead focuses primarily on pattern recognition, the algorithms need to be fine-tuned to remove biases. Processes should also be introduced to avoid the biases that we, humans, inevitably bring to the table.
- Privacy. It’s critical that developers consider how using AI may impact any personally identifiable information (PII) embedded in the data being processed. While AI processing does remove some privacy concerns in that it bypasses human interaction with sensitive data, it raises others, such as the scope of information use, where it is stored, and who can access it.
Proactive Approach To Ethical AI By The Technology Community
AI is here to stay and efforts to tame its power will surely follow. Thinking proactively, industry players are looking into ways to make sure their applications follow the frameworks that call for AI to be trustworthy, transparent, fair and ensure privacy. One way to ensure that is by using a peer review system. Here, AI developers would submit their use cases for review in an AI Community akin to open-source environments that came before.
Another way to add clarity to AI applications is to develop an ad hoc organization where companies would commit their projects and applications to a central AI Registry. Unlike a formal standards body that is typically dominated by large organizations that control the agenda, the registry would be a self-reporting body for gathering feedback, advice and affirmation. Ultimately, the best way to ensure that AI applications are deployed ethically might be to embed ethics in computer science curricula from the very start.

title: Could AI-Powered Silicon Remastering Be A Solution To The Chip Shortage?
text:
From the Beatles Let It Be to John Coltrane’s A Love Supreme and Radiohead’s OK Computer, record labels often remaster classic albums from the greats in many genres of music. These higher fidelity remasters are a welcome treat for aficionados and mainstream fans alike. But what if I told you, just like Led Zeppelin’s or Van Halen’s greatest hits, semiconductor chips could be “remastered” as well, and these remasters could help bail us out of the current chip shortage? For some folks that would totally rock, pun intended, but let’s take a step back and look at the problem and potential solutions at hand first.
Chip Re-Designs Are Costly And Take Too Much Time
The process of designing and verifying chips like the modern processors, controllers and sensors in cars, for example, can take years and require millions of dollars of R&D. Semiconductor mask sets alone (the photomasks that pattern circuit designs on silicon wafers) cost millions of dollars for leading-edge process nodes. And sometimes engineers don’t get designs right on the first try of course, where a chip bug could force a dreaded “re-spin” that may cost millions more.
As you might imagine, with the stakes this high in man-hours and resources, even major OEMs like Ford and General Motors can be hesitant to move legacy designs from older, capacity-constrained chip fabs, to new, more modern process nodes that have the much-needed spare capacity to handle big production runs. This dynamic flies in the face of the automotive industry’s need for supply chains that must produce chips sometimes for many years over the life cycle of a vehicle model or an entire fleet’s platform. And these dynamics aren’t going away anytime soon, with technology and silicon content becoming ever-more present in virtually all types of products, beyond just the automotive industry.
That said, the growth of chip content in vehicles is scaling perhaps at an even more rapid pace versus other industries, projected by major players like Intel, to comprise up to 20% of the BOM (Bill of Materials) in cars by the year 2030. There may, however, be at least a partial solution to this problem on the horizon, and it harnesses the power of our new, ever-advancing friends known as AI and machine learning.
This Is Tricky, Let’s Get The AI To Do It
To reiterate the high-level problem here, generally speaking, re-targeting old chip designs to a new modern manufacturing process nodes is both costly and time-consuming, but that’s where AI (Artificial Intelligence) could come to the rescue. To put it simply, the hyper-iterative nature of machine learning is well-suited for certain tasks in the semiconductor design process, especially the mundane grunt-work of optimization for performance, power and area (silicon real estate) of chip designs. As I covered back in December, chip design tools bellwether, Synopsys, is making great strides at harnessing machine learning in many areas of chip design, from place and route (otherwise known as floor-planning of circuits), to verification (proving out designs so they’re bug free before production) and even someday pulling-in the actual software workloads that will run on chips in an effort to help further optimize designs.
The latest AI-fueled innovation Synopsys has on tap is, you guessed it, Silicon Remastering of legacy chips in newer, more modern chip fab processes. The beauty of chip designs is that they’re all simulated and verified in various EDA (Electronic Design Automation) tools before they’re sent to produce mask sets and eventually the silicon wafer fab itself. Design engineers have been building chips in their own little metaverse this way for decades, with what is essentially a “digital twin” of the chip. Eventually, once a chip is well-simulated and fully validated, it’s then sent out for those costly next steps of fabrication.
To re-design an old chip for a new fab process in the traditional sense, however, requires a team of engineers and expensive re-spin costs, valuable manhours and long time-to-market windows; that is unless you could just feed that original design to the machine and ask it to target that fancy new 7nm (7 nanometer) process node. In fact, Synopsys claims its design remastering AI can not only retarget modern chip fab process nodes, but some day also provide derivative designs and full remakes as well.
In the example above, Synopsys is illustrating an actual customer design, where the red triangle represents a manual design effort of a team of human engineers. As you can see, the clock speed (Frequency) and power characteristics are significantly less optimal than the diamond targets achieved by the AI trained on an original source manufacturing node. Synopsys could then achieve even better performance and power characteristics as well, after training the AI with that same design on a more advanced chip fab process that has inherently better characteristics for speed and power efficiency.
The early results of this technology are very encouraging, and in concert with its IDM 2.0 chip fab and foundry service expansion, Intel is already getting on board with Synopsys Silicon Remastering. “Synopsys is a key design partner in our IFS Ecosystem Alliance. We are excited about the potential of technologies like Silicon Remastering to help Intel Foundry Services customers optimize their designs for PPA (Power, Performance, Area),” noted Bob Brennan, VP and GM of Intel Foundry Services.
Of course, Silicon Remastering also plays right into Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger’s hand, as he recently encouraged chip-starved automakers to, “rather than spend [ing] billions on new ‘old’ fabs, let’s spend millions to help migrate designs to modern ones.”
As such, it seems that there’s an excellent opportunity here for a solution to at least some of our current chip shortage issues in the short term. And it may lie in the idea of making something old new again, by remastering chips, just like we do with the great works of Jimi Hendrix or popular retro game titles with cult-like followings. Just toss that classic chip design over the wall to the AI and let it do its thing, so we can build it in a modern fab.

title: Digital Workers Are Toiling Away At A Bank Near You
text:
In the early days of automation and AI, vendors rarely mentioned the possibility of smart machines replacing human beings. Jobs were not going to be automated out of existence; instead they were going to be augmented, with machines doing the boring tasks and humans freed to do more creative and interesting work. Virtually every vendor of AI and automation systems adopted this mantra. And it was mostly correct; AI and robotic process automation (RPA) generally automated tasks, not entire jobs, so at most any human job loss was on the margins.
2022, however, is the year of the Great Resignation. It can be argued whether or not job departures are historically high, but the broad perception is that human labor is in short supply. As a result, there is less concern at the moment that AI and automation will present pink slips to humans.
One company, WorkFusion, has decided that this is the time to provide digital workers as eventual replacements for, not just adjuncts to, human workers. The company was the first back in 2015 to offer the combination of RPA and machine learning, known even then as “intelligent automation.” Now it is offering a set of digital workers that use that same combination of technologies. The digital workers, which you can view here (they look a lot like humans!), are each focused on a particular set of tasks. WorkFusion argues that they comprise full jobs (at least administrative and monitoring jobs), not just tasks, though I suspect that will vary across organizations. And WorkFusion does say that the digital workers will need human review over their decisions, at least at the beginning of their employment in a company. The jobs currently performed by the six digital workers (each of which have been given names and suitably diverse photos) include:
- Insurance underwriter
- Banking customer identity program analyst
- Banking entity sanctions screening analyst
- Banking transactions screening analyst
- Banking due diligence program analyst
- Customer service coordinator (email and portal inquiries)
These do all sound like full jobs, although the WorkFusion website says that the insurance underwriter can do perhaps 70% of the human underwriter role. That’s consistent with my previous research on a human digital underwriter—easy decisions are handled by an AI system, but the hard ones require an experienced human eye. The other digital worker jobs seem to require less human expertise.
The Flexible, Learning Digital Worker
Adam Famularo, the new CEO of WorkFusion, told me that the digital workers can be owned or rented by the transaction, and can come on premise (probably won’t catch COVID there!) or be cloud-based. He said that the workers would become smarter over time—that the machine learning models within them would be retrained from the data captured by each worker deployed at a customer. He also said that new digital workers could be created by customers and partners, and that WorkFusion would eventually operate a “digital worker exchange.”
Famularo spoke to a large number of customers when he assumed the job, and he said that none were worried about the job loss issue. Many brought up the shortage of labor they were experiencing. All of the customers, he told me, reported that they have human employees working alongside digital workers, or humans who were redeployed to other work. He feels that most of the jobs performed by the digital workers thus far are pretty tedious, and that no human would miss them much. He did say, however, that he was hearing a lot about digital labor as a replacement for outsourcing.
Digital Workers at Bank of Montreal
To understand how a customer is using these digital workers, I spoke with Adam Schabes, who is the US Chief Anti-Money Laundering (AML) Officer at Bank of Montreal (BMO). He confirmed that digital workers are already supporting key AML activities at BMO, including sanction screening—checking to see if clients are on or doing business with sanctioned individuals or countries on various government-provided lists. A human employee still makes the final determination, but the administrative research tasks are done by the digital worker. The digital sanction screening worker, whom WorkFusion named Evelyn, visits external websites and various applications in the bank to find out who the bank shouldn’t be doing business with. “Our employees who previously did this type of work had investigation backgrounds, but you don’t need that background to go through lists—it’s an administrative exercise,” Schabes said.
BMO is also in the process of standing up Tara, a digital worker from WorkFusion that does transaction screening. Like sanction screening, it’s an administrative task to which a digital worker is well suited. The content turned up by Tara can go directly into the Suspicious Activity Reports the bank has to supply to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network. The combination of work by Evelyn, Tara, and other machine learning models that BMO has employed have all helped to reduce the number of false positive suspicious events that humans have to investigate by 25% or so.
Overall, Schabes said, the digital workers from WorkFusion have been pretty successful. At first, he said, his staff had a lot of apprehension about job security. After they saw how the digital workers performed the relatively menial tasks, however, morale was boosted in the department. People started to ask, “Can the robots also take on this task?” Some requests had to be turned down so as not to overload them. Human workers have been able to move to more client-facing and revenue-generating activity as a result of being freed up from the tedious administrative work.
The AML staff had actually begun to name their RPA robots before the digital worker concept was introduced by WorkFusion—they called the first one “Becky.” Someone even put a cardboard box with a face on it and tinfoil arms on a desk to represent Becky. This isn’t the first time I have heard of software robots being anthropomorphized; we humans seem to like the idea of them once we get used to it.
Schabes concluded, “We are looking to do more of this,” and I strongly doubt that he will be alone in that attitude. Particularly in banking and insurance, there is a lot of back-office work that machines can do pretty easily. First there was RPA, then there was intelligent automation, and now there are full-fledged digital workers. At the moment I don’t think that most human employees have much to fear from the current crop of digital workers, but who knows what will come next?

title: Council Post: Can AI Appreciate The Beauty Of Artwork?
text:
Co-founder & Chief AI Officer at Kellify - Entrepreneur and adjunct professor of Predictive methods for the Enterprise at Genoa University.
In recent years, artificial intelligence has become more and more important in the development of artwork. In 2018, the first artwork "painted" by an AI program was sold at an auction for $432,500.
In light of this, is it possible for AI to be able to discern what is beautiful or develop its own taste in artwork? In order to answer this question, we first have to create AI that can evaluate the price of different pieces of art with the same degree of accuracy as human experts. My company did just this with a team of researchers.
Evaluating Beauty
After months of development, AI models were able to look at eight Pierre-Auguste Renoir paintings — all from the same time period and of similar canvas size. Human experts gave those paintings a range of prices, starting in the mere hundreds of euros per square centimeter and ending at 1,763 euros per square centimeter. We had to ask, why only 110 euros per square centimeter for one of them? The answer from human experts? This art is ugly!
Being "ugly" is not necessarily a measurable trait. It's a highly volatile qualifier, and it can vary over time for a multitude of reasons, trends, customs and traditions. This uncertainty is reflected in most areas of art investment, resulting in a low willingness to invest in lesser-known artists and the like.
This is where AI comes in: There is an emerging market where artwork needs to be evaluated without exposing it to human bias. But can beauty become something measurable?
We started by evaluating which metrics can measure beauty in a data-centric world:
• The art's "likes" on social media, online museums and online exhibitions. This is a good measure of the average appreciation for a specific piece of artwork, measured by the entire audience of an online gallery.
• The art's value compared to the artist's average artwork price. This gives us a look at the average appreciation for a piece of art measured by experts and art lovers who know the given artist well.
• The art's realized price compared to its estimated price in auctions. Sometimes realized prices are higher than estimates. This can give us insight into the value given to art by buyers and sellers.
Training an AI model on these parameters allows it to better define the intrinsic value of a piece of artwork. It can find similarities between different pieces of "liked" artwork within a given set and detect what might be appreciated about them and what might not.
Is AI Completely Without Bias?
Is this definition of beauty affected by human bias still? Absolutely. People who browse online art events are just a subset of the population. That being said, our aim was to help those investing in art make better decisions within a biased environment, not evaluate an absolute standard of beauty.
Beauty will forever remain an exquisitely human qualifier that will always beget variability in this market. AI can, however, start to better capture the intrinsic value of artwork to limit market uncertainty.
Designing With Bias In Mind
When designing a machine learning program like we did, it's important to make sure you can train it with numeric data. If your goal involves non-numeric data, then a machine learning approach won't be sufficient. From there, you're able to create a program that learns from data in an effort to simulate human cognitive processes. In our case, we aimed to simulate how humans process aesthetic recognition.
Bias is always present in AI projects. In our case, the artwork market is based on the judgment of a minority (art collectors, art advisors, gallerists and others), while the judgment of the majority has very little importance. We had to evaluate how to balance data from the minority (auction prices) with data from the majority ("likes" in virtual museums). In other words, we deliberately exploited a bias because we knew how much biases influence the art market.
It's necessary to evaluate biases like this when building your own AI systems. Otherwise, you won't be able to reproduce estimations with that same level of bias.

title: Council Post: Ways For Insurers To Incorporate And Collaborate With Insurtech
text:
Founder & CEO at Indus Net Technologies (INT.) — Delivering #DigitalSuccess at the confluence of technology, analytics & marketing.
We are living in an era where digitalization has reshaped almost every aspect of our lives, and the insurance industry is no exception. Gone are the days when people filled out manual forms and filed paperwork to buy insurance policies.
Instead, buying insurance policies has become a cakewalk thanks to insurtech, a portmanteau of the words insurance and technology. Put simply, insurtech is the concept of implementing technologies like artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT) and machine learning (ML) in the insurance industry.
As many have recognized, the pandemic has further forced the rapid growth of end-to-end digital services of insurers. Nowadays, you can receive customized insurance products with the help of big data and smart devices. However, in this market of continuously changing customer demand and increasing internet adoption, forecasting consumer behavior is becoming difficult as practically any data piece might be significant.
Insurtech firms can help effectively utilize this vast amount of data. A survey commissioned by Capgemini reveals that more than 75% of insurers admit that they are considering insurtech collaboration to improve their customer experiences.
There are certain methods that I have seen in which insurance companies can incorporate insurtech. But first, although insurtech has changed the industry as a whole, here are some specific areas where I see it has made some of its most significant impacts and where you can focus your efforts.
Offering Bite-Sized Insurances
People who were not comfortable paying a considerable amount for annual premiums every year are finding interest in bite-sized insurances. Insurtech is helping successfully sell insurances for specific requirements like Covid-19, vector-borne diseases, etc.
A large population of millennials are uninsured. Hence, they are a potentially lucrative sector for insurers. As a whole, they prefer insurance policies that are easy to buy and require less paperwork. For example, Acko, a digital-native insurer in India, has collaborated with almost 20 digital platforms to expand its business. Ethos is another example of a digital-native insurance company. They recently received around $200 million and then shortly after another $100 million in venture capital. Although not entirely digital, other insurance companies like Ageas Insurance, one of my company’s clients, are utilizing fully customized and integrated ecosystems to manage the user journey more quickly and accurately.
Using Robotic Process Automation In The Insurance Industry
Robotic process automation (RPA) is a type of software bot that can execute rule-based and repetitive tasks quickly with more accuracy. Once bots are programmed to execute a task, they will follow the same steps every time.
RPA can help in faster processing of claims, underwriting, policy cancellation and data entry works. Besides, RPA creates a wide range of cross-selling opportunities as chatbots can suggest customized insurance products by extracting data from a customer’s profile.
Implementing Artificial Intelligence (AI)
A Business Line report says that insurance frauds in India cost ₹45,000 crores every year to insurers. Insurers face the challenge of faster claim processing for genuine customers and rejecting fraudulent claims. AI can find any discrepancies in claims or erroneous information provided by customers.
The basic difference between RPA and AI is that RPA is process centric and AI is data centric. You need to train RPA to execute a process, and it will follow that data for repeating tasks. On the other hand, AI can process unstructured data by creating its own logic and taking immediate action.
A Changing Industry
Many insurance companies already have a customer base and have been operating for a long time. But they will still need to utilize insurtech and insurtech services to meet the changing needs of customers and improve operational efficiency.
Insurance companies need to understand that the habits and perspectives of people have changed with time. So, first, insurers need to remove the tag of “agent only companies.” And focus on the DIY model, which the insurtechs promote.
Secondly, people prefer to buy insurance policies for specific needs like travel, high-end electronic devices, etc. So, insurance companies should come up with sachet policies to cater to the trending clientele.
Ways To Implement Fintech
After deploying insurtech techniques, insurance companies should be able to observe certain changes to ensure that their policies have been successful. Here are a few examples to look for:
• Better risk management by using data points of analytics and machine learning.
• Improved client satisfaction as claims are likely to be processed faster.
• Reduction in premium amounts due to the lower underwriting costs.
• Lower costs along with high profitability due to effective fraud prevention will increase the revenue of the insurer.
• Insurers will see an improvement in customer outreach and web presence.
There are also some common challenges that insurers might face during the transition to insurtech. According to a global survey of insurance CEOs conducted by KPMG International, these include: lack of insight into the future of operational scenarios, difficulties making quick technology-related decisions and challenges in moving from pilots and experiments to scaled deployment.
To overcome these challenges, here are my insights:
• Insurance companies need to find out how many IT experts they will require for implementing insurtech. Otherwise, it’s going to be a mammoth task.
• Insurance companies need to get rid of their legacy systems as they can be potential roadblocks to implementing insurtech systems.
• An insurer should train its employees with the recent technology trends so that they feel comfortable with the transition and empowered to maximize the company’s ROI.
• An insurance company should chalk out its budgetary limitations on how much it can afford for implementing insurtech.
So, the bottom line is customers want everything at their convenience and are technology-driven. Young and millennial customers, along with older adults too, want to get insured by a company that is digital and offers customized products. It’s high time for insurers to collaborate with and incorporate insurtech.

title: Reflections On a Decade Of AI
text:
Recently, I was asked to be the General Co-Chair for the IEEE International Conference on Connected Vehicles (ICCVE). Founded a decade ago with academic roots, the 2022 version extended beyond the academic model with a significant industry and regulatory emphasis, and concurrent physical locations in Shanghai, Pune, and Munich. Interestingly, the decade-long historical backdrop of the conference and the assembly of the worldwide activity provided an opportunity to be reflective about progress beyond the noise from the tactical day-to-day headlines.
Where do we really stand with AI technology? How did we get here? The next few articles will consist of some reflections of the past, present, and future of this technology.
Historically, the fundamental technology and approach of “intelligence” has been a shifting paradigm. In the early days of AI, intelligence was derived by a symbolic manipulation of objects in the era of “Symbolic AI.” Somewhat akin to the difference between algebra (symbol) and arithmetic (numbers), these systems had an engine which would manipulate symbols until a goal was reached. Using this methodology, many interesting problems could be solved, but the problems which could be solved were of limited size.
The next wave consisted of the age of “Expert Systems” where a series of human developed rules were developed to solve a particular problem and the underlying engine sifted through the rules in order to reach a solution. The introduction of human developed rules solved many of the size limitations of the previous approach, but also created a large dependency on human developed data. Both of these approaches significantly moved forward the state-of-art, but unfortunately were victims of the hype cycle with the result of “AI Winters.”
In the last decade, “intelligence” has been redefined again with terms such as deep learning. Recognizing the inherent limitation of a process which involves human “programming,” deep learning has built a “learning” paradigm. In this paradigm, there is a period of training where the AI machine “learns” from data to build its own rules. Learning is defined using traditional mathematical optimization algorithms which try to minimize some notion of error. Getting past the machinery, the thought process behind the model itself is fairly profound and somewhat unique.
The process of simply giving data to an engine and automatically developing an algorithm has the feeling of a magic elixir. However, the technique does seem to “work” in areas such as vision or natural language processing where conventional solutions have been difficult. This contrast between conventional deterministic computer science and machine learning was explored in an article “Is Machine Learning The Quantum Physics Of Computer Science ?” where an analogy is built to conventional Einsteinian physics and Quantum Physics. Similar to Quantum Physics, a collective understanding of the power as well as limitations of machine learning techniques are being developed. Table 1 below discusses some of the learnings after a decade of the contrasts between these two approaches to algorithmic development.
After a decade, where do we stand?
ML algorithms are seen as the vital critical new tool which can enable the next wave of electronics driven innovation. There are unquestioned successes in fields such as search, recommendation systems, and increasingly language processing. Significant investment has been expended in the area of autonomy with some success. However, several open questions remain:
- Safety Critical Systems: With words such as non-deterministic, not analyzable, not theoryful, how can one build and most importantly verify safety critical systems?
- Computational Complexity: If one cannot evaluate computational complexity, how can one be assured that one can converge onto a solution. Said another way: Will Tesla’s Dojo significantly move the state-of-art or is it a white elephant dependent on the wrong fundamental algorithm?
- Underlying Computational Fabric: Tesla Dojo and many other applications have centered on the Nvidia computational model. Is this the right computational structure or is it limiting to progress? Are there interesting alternatives ?
Over the last decade, the answers to some of these questions are coming into focus and will be explored in subsequent articles.

title: Graphcore Launches 3rd-Gen AI With Wafer-On-Wafer (WoW!) Technology
text:
Startup also teases $120M Brain-Scale AI “Good Computer” For 2024
Remember Intel’s old Tick-Tock processor roadmap? The company alternated between two approaches, bringing out a new generation featuring architectural enhancements, then subsequently shrinking that chip into a new smaller process node. Both approaches typically deliver about 15% better performance. Historically these are the two approaches chip makers have always had at their disposal to keep on the Moore’s Law train.
But now there is a third approach being pioneered by AI unicorn Graphcore and TSMC. The idea is to use two stacked wafers, one with the Graphcore Colossus logic die and one for efficient power delivery. Then TSMC slices the double wafer into dies for normal packaging, in contrast to the full-sized wafer approach of another startup, Cerebras.
What is a BOW IPU?
Basically, Graphcore developed a new version of the Colossus chip, used in the 2nd generation IPU, that has power connectivity to the sandwiched 2nd power delivery wafer. This approach connects the transistors to power over far shorter distances compared to the traditional power regulators alongside the chip’s package. By adding deep trench capacitors in the power delivery die, right next to the processing cores and memory, Graphcore is able to deliver power much more efficiently – enabling 350 TeraFLOPS of AI compute and delivering nearly 40% more performance across a wide range of AI models, all at 16% better power efficiency.
Graphcore’s resulting new BOW Intelligence Processing Unit (IPU) delivers better performance without any programmer-visible changes to the chip’s logic, and without requiring a new manufacturing process node. All this translates to lower development costs for Graphcore, faster time to market, and zero code changes for developers. To our knowledge, this has never been attempted nor accomplished in a commercially-available semiconductor.
As for system configurations, Graphcore was able to convert all their existing PODs to BOW, thanks to the compatibility with the existing IPU Machine. Also, Graphcore said that there is no increase in pricing, which will further extend what the company claims is superior price/performance leadership. The flagship Bow Pod256 delivers more than 89 PetaFLOPS of AI compute, while the Bow POD1024 delivers 350 PetaFLOPS of AI compute, with enough memory across the complex to handle the largest AI models currently in development.
In a welcome change, Graphcore included references to customers who already have access to the new platform, including several cloud service providers and Pacific Northwest National Labs. “For instance, we are pursuing applications in computational chemistry and cybersecurity applications. This year, Graphcore systems have allowed us to significantly reduce both training and inference times from days to hours for these applications,” said Sutanay Choudhury, co-director of PNNL's Computational and Theoretical Chemistry Institute
What, and Who, is “Good”?
Back in 1965, the computer science pioneer Jack Good was the first person to describe a machine that would exceed the capability of our brain in his paper, Speculations Concerning the First Ultra-Intelligent Machine. In honor of this pioneer, Graphcore has named it’s first planned Exa-scale AI system the “Good Computer”, a system that would exceed the human brain in terms of the number of parameters, or synapses. Other companies including NVIDIA and Cerebras have outlined their plans for brain-scale computing as well so this level of computation is already moving from fantasy to reality.
While the company didn’t disclose technology details, it did share that they expect this system to deliver over 10 Exa-Flops of AI floating-point compute capacity, with 4 petabytes of memory over 10 petabytes/second of memory bandwidth, and support for AI models of up to 500 trillion parameters. The system would cost about $120 million. Since there is no way Graphcore would build this speculatively, it is safe to assume they have several prospective clients lined up to buy and run one of these beasts. Otherwise, Graphcore would be foolish to announce these plans only to disappoint the market and investors in just two years.
What are the implications for the industry?
Surely, TSMC is already exploring other customers for the WoW technology, and we expect that effort will be successful. Getting 40% better performance without taping out a new architecture or to a new, smaller manufacturing node is astounding. Moreover, we believe that this wafer stacking technique represents many more opportunities beyond power delivery. <Speculation On> One could imagine, for example, that I/O could be added to the second wafer, or perhaps in the longer term logic could be added in a third wafer for amazing density and performance, if one can figure out how to cool it. And the potential of combining the multi-wafer approach with full wafer-scale devices a la Cerebras makes our heads spin <Speculation Off>.
Conclusions
Clearly the emergence and value of heterogeneous computation and acceleration has opened up a Pandora’s box of new approaches to silicon design and manufacturing. We believe that Graphcore has begun to cross the chasm, with customers now going on-the-record with significant results. Yes, NVIDIA is still the champion, especially in software and per-device performance. But Graphcore is steadily finding its own niches where it can shine brightly. And the WoW technology appears to have significant promise that will be fun to watch!

My firm, Cambrian AI Research, is fortunate to have many, if not most, semiconductor firms as our clients, including Blaize, Cerebras, Esperanto, Graphcore, IBM, Intel, NVIDIA, Qualcomm Technologies, Synopsys, and Tenstorrent. We have no investment positions in any of the companies mentioned in this article and do not plan to initiate any in the near future.
